source: Hoffmann and Nebel (2001) The FF Planning System: Fast Plan Generation Through Heuristic Search (JAIR 14)
finding: FF estimates goal distance by solving the delete-relaxed problem (a relaxed plan from Graphplan), then adds enforced hill-climbing and helpful-action pruning. It was the best automatic planner at AIPS-2000.
numbers: 20 benchmark domains tested. FF 'extremely competitive' on 16 of 20. Only 'satisfying' on the two Blocksworlds, Mprime and Mystery. Grid (5 tasks): FF 0.15, 0.47, 2.11, 1.93, 19.54 s vs GRT 1.04 to 118.65 s. Assembly: FF solves 25 of 30 tasks in under 5 s; IPP4.0 solves only 4 small ones, up to 12 h.
limits: Own-lab benchmarks on a 350 MHz Sparc; competition domains are 'simple' by the authors' own admission. Not a controlled ablation of relaxation alone.
agent_relevance: The relaxed estimate is only a ranking signal for a greedy search. Its worth comes from being cheap to compute, not from being exact.

source: Hoffmann and Nebel (2001) The FF Planning System (JAIR 14), section 8.2 on where FF is weak
finding: On Mystery and Mprime (Logistics with fuel limits) FF fails on many tasks because the relaxation cannot see dead ends such as running out of fuel. Random restarts of the search did not help. The older Lisp planner Unpop solved tasks FF could not.
numbers: Unpop solved four Mystery and three Mprime tasks that FF did not. In every unsolved task FF's hill-climbing ended in a dead end, whatever randomization was tried. Complete best-first fallback ran out of memory on larger tasks.
limits: Authors state the cause as an explanation ('we think'), not a tested result. Unpop is in Lisp, so times are not comparable.
agent_relevance: Core boundary condition. A relaxation that drops a constraint (delete lists, fuel use) is blind to dead ends created by that constraint. Our agent must keep a hard check on the dropped constraint before it commits.

source: Hoffmann and Nebel (2001) The FF Planning System (JAIR 14), Elevator and Briefcase results
finding: Relaxed-plan search gives non-optimal but near-optimal plans, and helpful-action pruning keeps only a small fraction of successors.
numbers: Miconic-ADL: FF plan length within 133% of optimal at most, 111% on average (vs PropPlan optimal). Helpful actions average about 15% of successors. Breadth-first escape rarely deeper than 4 or 5 steps. Briefcase: FF solves 11-object tasks in under 1 s; IPP fails for 7 or more objects.
limits: Runtime varies widely when hill-climbing hits a dead end and falls back to best-first.
agent_relevance: Solve the relaxed problem to propose a short list of promising moves, then act on that list. Use the full model only to verify.

source: Hoffmann (2005) Where 'Ignoring Delete Lists' Works: Local Search Topology in Planning Benchmarks (JAIR 24)
finding: Proves, for the ideal relaxed heuristic h+, which benchmark domains have easy search landscapes. Many have no unrecognized dead ends and bounded plateau escape, which explains why delete relaxation works so well on them.
numbers: 30 domains studied. 24 have no unrecognized dead ends. In 17 of those 24, the exit distance from local minima is bounded by a constant (13 have no local minima at all). In 12 of those 17, the exit distance from benches is also constant, so FF's search is polynomial given h+.
quote: Many of the 30 investigated domains lie in classes where h+ is a provably high-quality heuristic
limits: Proofs are for ideal h+ (NP-hard to compute), not for the h_FF approximation. Domain by domain, not a general theorem. 6 of 30 domains have unrecognized dead ends.
agent_relevance: Relaxation quality is a property of the problem class, not of the method. Before trusting a relaxed estimate, our agent should ask whether the problem has dead ends the relaxation hides.

source: Hoffmann (2005) Where 'Ignoring Delete Lists' Works, section 5.2 empirical check of h_FF against h+
finding: The practical approximation h_FF mostly keeps the good landscape that h+ has. This checks the theory against the real heuristic by sampling states.
numbers: 20 domains. In 11 domains where h+ has no local minima, 230 groups of random instances: 220 groups had zero valley states, 8 groups under 1.0%, one group 2.2%, one group 5.0%. Grid and Hanoi were the exceptions. Across bounded-bench domains one sampled state had exit distance 2 instead of 1 (Logistics). 100 states sampled per instance.
limits: Sampling, not exhaustive. 10 IPC-3 and IPC-4 domains not included in the empirical part. Author's own earlier experiments (Hoffmann 2001b, 2003b).
agent_relevance: A cheap approximate relaxed solve can inherit the good properties of the exact one, but this has to be checked per domain.

source: Helmert and Domshlak (2009) Landmarks, Critical Paths and Abstractions: What's the Difference Anyway? (ICAPS)
finding: Compares the four families of heuristics (delete relaxation, critical paths, abstractions, landmarks) by dominance. Landmark heuristics and additive hmax dominate each other. Merge-and-shrink abstractions strictly dominate both. Pattern databases are incomparable with them.
numbers: Pairwise dominance results for admissible heuristics. Applies only to relaxation-based landmarks.
quote: Pattern database abstractions are incomparable with landmark heuristics and additive hmax heuristics.
limits: Theory is about admissible heuristics, with restrictions. Dominance in estimate does not mean faster search, since cost per node differs.
agent_relevance: No single way of simplifying a problem is best. Different relaxations see different structure, so a portfolio of two or three simplifications is justified.

source: Helmert and Domshlak (2009) Landmarks, Critical Paths and Abstractions, experiments with the landmark-cut heuristic
finding: The new LM-cut heuristic, built from the relaxation view, gives the most accurate admissible estimates tested. It solves more tasks than the landmark heuristic h_LA, even where both estimate h+ perfectly at the start, because it recomputes information at every state.
numbers: LM-cut with A* solved 450 tasks vs 422 for h_LA; next planner Gamer 312. LM-cut best or near-best in 16 of 22 domains. Perfect h+ estimate on at least 72% of tasks. Mean error of h_LA 1.94, about 7 times that of LM-cut; relative error 3.8 times higher. Blocks: 43 to 48 times fewer expansions on the two largest common tasks. Exceptions: Gripper, FreeCell; Openstacks, where hmax was best because it is cheapest per node.
limits: IPC-2008 optimal track only. Authors compare accuracy against h+-based heuristics only, not against the true cost.
agent_relevance: Recomputing the relaxed estimate at every new state beats computing it once at the start. For our agent: re-solve the simple version after each step, do not reuse the first estimate.

source: Helmert and Roger (2008) How Good is Almost Perfect? (AAAI 2008, best paper)
finding: Even a nearly perfect heuristic (error bounded by a small constant) does not remove exponential search for A* in common domains, including Gripper and Miconic, which are easy to solve in polynomial time. Better heuristics alone hit a wall.
numbers: Proofs for a number of benchmark domains: exponential node expansions under an additive error bound c. Authors argue for other enhancements such as symmetry elimination or domain simplification.
quote: improve a heuristic search algorithm by refining its heuristic estimates is basically fruitless
limits: Worst-case argument for optimal A* search, not satisficing greedy search. The satisficing results in b01 and b04 are a different regime.
agent_relevance: When the goal is the best answer (optimal), improving the estimate has diminishing returns. When any good answer is enough, a rough relaxed estimate is already enough.

source: Korf (1997) Finding Optimal Solutions to Rubik's Cube Using Pattern Databases (AAAI-97)
finding: Abstraction heuristic: store the exact solution length of a simplified puzzle (only corner cubies, or six edge cubies) in a lookup table and use it as a lower bound. This made the first optimal solutions of random Rubik's Cube instances possible.
numbers: Ten random instances solved optimally. Median optimal length 18 moves. Three tables, 82 MB total, about 1 hour to build. Searches to depth 16 average 9.5 billion nodes, under 4 hours. Depth 17 averages 122 billion nodes, about 2 days. Table lookup runs at about 700,000 nodes per second, 7000 times faster than computing the heuristic on the fly (100 nodes per second).
limits: Only 10 instances. One puzzle with strong symmetry structure. Paid with large memory and hours of precomputation.
agent_relevance: A simplified problem that is solved exactly and cached beats a rough estimate computed again each time. For us: keep a reusable library of solved simple cases.

source: Helmert (2006) The Fast Downward Planning System (JAIR 26)
finding: Uses a causal-graph heuristic, which solves simplified subproblems of the task, together with the FF heuristic and preferred operators. Best configuration: multi-heuristic best-first search with preferred operators (M+P).
numbers: M+P: no other configuration solves more tasks in 23 of 29 domains. Preferred operators help in 10 domains vs worse in 5 (greedy search) and 15 vs 2 (multi-heuristic). Fast Downward won IPC4 non-optimizing track. Weak domains: Pipesworld (not hierarchical), Promela-OpticalTelegraph, Schedule.
limits: Compared in the author's own lab. The paper notes FF beats it on some domain groups; the winner differs by domain.
agent_relevance: Two different simplifications used together beat either alone. Also a hint to rank moves with the simple solve and expand the favored ones first.

source: Richter and Westphal (2010) The LAMA Planner: Guiding Cost-Based Anytime Planning with Landmarks (JAIR 39)
finding: Landmarks (facts that must hold in every plan) combined with the FF relaxed-plan heuristic improved results, but the landmark heuristic alone was not competitive. Making the estimate cost-sensitive did not pay off.
numbers: Best planner in IPC 2008 sequential satisficing track. Landmark-only configurations: IPC score 164 to 167 and 185 to 189 coverage, vs scores above 194 and coverage above 223 for configurations that also use FF/add. Landmarks plus iterated weighted A* gave 2 extra score points on first solutions but 9 on final ones (synergy). Cost-unaware search was at least about equal, often better, than cost-sensitive.
limits: IPC 2008 domains only (9 domains, 30 tasks each). Landmarks hurt solution quality in Openstacks for first solutions.
agent_relevance: Landmarks (must-do subgoals) are a useful add-on to a relaxed estimate, not a replacement. Also: adding more detail into the estimate (costs) did not help, so keep the simple version simple.

source: Valmeekam, Marquez, Sreedharan, Kambhampati (2023) On the Planning Abilities of Large Language Models: A Critical Investigation (NeurIPS 2023)
finding: LLMs alone almost never produce executable plans. As a heuristic source (LLM plan used as a seed that a sound planner repairs) the gain is modest but real. As a human aid it was not significant.
numbers: Average autonomous success about 3%. LPG repair of LLM plans: mean Levenshtein edit distance 7.22 against final plan length 11.7 over 600 instances. Human study: 17 of 23 (74%) without help vs 18 of 22 (82%) with LLM suggestion, not significant. Blocksworld GPT-3 Instruct: 41/600 plan generation (6.8%).
limits: Older models (GPT-3 family, Instruct-GPT3). Small user study. Plans were repaired by a sound planner, so the LLM was not the verifier.
agent_relevance: An LLM's draft is a rough relaxed plan at best: useful as a start for a checked repair step, not as a final answer.

source: Valmeekam et al. (2023) PlanBench (NeurIPS 2023 Datasets and Benchmarks), appendix A.4.2 relaxation analysis
finding: The authors judged GPT-4's plans against delete-relaxed, precondition-relaxed and both-relaxed versions of Blocksworld. Even the most forgiving check left many plans invalid. So errors are not just missed side effects.
numbers: GPT-4 Blocksworld plan generation 206/600 correct (34.3%); Instruct-GPT3 41/600 (6.8%); cost-optimal 198/600 (33%); plan verification 191/600 (31.8%). Relaxed-model results are in Figure 5 (read as a chart, no exact counts in text).
quote: even in the most relaxed version of the evaluation, GPT-4 still fails in a lot of instances
limits: Used for failure analysis, not as a search guide. Exact relaxed percentages are only in a figure.
agent_relevance: The failures are deeper than ignoring negative effects. Telling a model to 'ignore the side effects' will not fix its planning errors.

source: Valmeekam, Stechly, Kambhampati (2024) LLMs Still Can't Plan; Can LRMs? A Preliminary Evaluation of OpenAI's o1 on PlanBench
finding: o1 jumps ahead of LLMs on 3 to 5 block Blocksworld, but accuracy collapses with obfuscated names, longer plans, and unsolvable instances. Classical planners stay at 100%.
numbers: o1-preview Blocksworld 97.8%; Mystery Blocksworld 52.8%; Randomized Mystery 37.3%; harder 20 to 40 step instances 23.63% (110 instances). Best LLM, Llama 3.1 405B, 62.6% zero-shot on Blocksworld; GPT-4 about 34% earlier. Unsolvable instances: o1 flagged only 27% correctly (16% on randomized mystery). Cost $1897.55 for the o1 experiments. Fast Downward 100%.
limits: o1-preview only, closed model, single paper. One-shot was not always better than zero-shot.
agent_relevance: Strong gain from extra inference-time reasoning, but it does not give the soundness a relaxed-plus-checked method has. Keep an external verifier.

source: Valmeekam, Marquez, Kambhampati (2023) Can Large Language Models Really Improve by Self-critiquing Their Own Plans?
finding: GPT-4 as its own plan verifier is unreliable. Self-critique loops do worse than a sound external checker.
numbers: 100 Blocksworld instances. Generator alone 40/100. LLM generator + LLM verifier with back-prompting 55/100. LLM + VAL (sound verifier) 88/100. LLM verifier accuracy 61%; it called 38 of 45 wrong plans valid (false-positive rate 84.45%). Type of feedback (binary vs detailed) mattered little; with VAL it was 74% (binary) vs 86% (detailed), n=50.
limits: 100 instances, one domain, GPT-4 (2023). The abstract says self-critique 'appears to diminish' performance; the table still shows 40 to 55 from critique, so the loss is vs the sound verifier.
agent_relevance: Any check of a relaxed answer against the real constraints must be done by a program or a strictly separate check, not by the same model rereading its own work (links to G-guardrails on verification).

source: Stechly, Valmeekam, Kambhampati (2024) Chain of Thoughtlessness? An Analysis of CoT in Planning
finding: Prompting with worked step-by-step examples helps only when the example is very close to the test problem class, and the gain fades as problems grow past the example size. This is a boundary on 'show it the easy version first'.
numbers: GPT-4, GPT-4-Turbo, Claude-3-Opus on Blocksworld with increasing block count. Meaningful gains only for the most specific prompts (table-to-stack, stacking). Gains decay as the number of blocks passes the size shown in examples. Sound planners such as Fast Downward: 100% on all sizes tested.
limits: Simple domain; no single headline percentage in the text I read; read from curves in figures.
agent_relevance: Solving the easy version first transfers only if the harder case really has the same structure. Our agent should state why the easy case maps to the hard one.

source: Corrêa, Pereira, Seipp (2025) Classical Planning with LLM-Generated Heuristics: Challenging the State of the Art with Python Code (NeurIPS 2025)
finding: Ask an LLM to write a domain-specific heuristic function as Python code, test 25 samples on training tasks, keep the best, and run it inside a sound greedy search. This beat end-to-end LLM planning by a wide margin and also beat h_FF.
numbers: 8 IPC-2023 learning-track domains, 90 test tasks each (720 total), test tasks much larger than training. End-to-end: Gemini 2.0 Flash 19, Flash Thinking 202, DeepSeek V3 48, R1 174 solved. LLM heuristic in Pyperplan GBFS: Flash 296, Flash Thinking 305, V3 343, R1 distill 214, R1 373. Baselines in Pyperplan: blind h0 120, h_FF 243. Cost: $0.25 (V3) and $6.12 (R1) for all heuristics.
limits: The paper text says h_FF solves 234 but its tables say 243; the table number is used here. Heuristic selection used training tasks only; the best of all 25 per prompt scored 423 vs 305 chosen (Gemini Flash Thinking ablation), so selection leaves much unused. Small models (R1 distill 14B) fall below h_FF.
agent_relevance: The strongest measured use of an LLM with heuristics: LLM writes the estimate once, a sound search uses it. Gains of 6x to 15x for non-reasoning models over asking them for the plan directly.

source: Corrêa, Pereira, Seipp (2025), comparison with C++ planners and robustness checks
finding: The LLM-written heuristic in slow Python matched the best learned domain-specific heuristic and beat classical relaxation heuristics in C++, and it was not simple memory recall.
numbers: Fast Downward total coverage (720 tasks): goal count 294, landmark count 295, h_FF 295, h_cea 306, h_cg 318, h_add 324, learned h_WGPLRF 371. Pyperplan with DeepSeek R1 heuristic 373, V3 343. Obfuscated Blocksworld: h_FF 27 to 28 (unchanged), R1 heuristic 66 down to 40. New domain Rod-Rings (never published): o3 heuristic 58 tasks vs h_FF 59. Spanner variant with non-breaking spanners: best heuristic was perfect.
limits: Own benchmark choice; Floortile was the one domain where h_FF was better. The R1 heuristic expanded fewer states in some domains but was worse in others; coverage gain partly from cheaper computation. Obfuscation cuts R1 coverage by about 40%, so token meaning matters.
agent_relevance: The model can build a good simplified estimate by reasoning about structure, but it leans on names. Our agent should rename or restate the problem in neutral terms before building a relaxation.

source: Corrêa, Pereira, Seipp (2025), prompt ablation (Table 4)
finding: What in the prompt matters for getting good heuristics: the domain description most, and example heuristics are essential. Without example domain-dependent heuristics, every generated heuristic scored 0.
numbers: Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking, 25 heuristics per variant, each run on the full test set. Best coverage: original 423, no long instructions 359, other single-component removals 368 to 404, no checklist 382. Worst coverage: original 114, no checklist 63. Mean coverage: original 267.0 (sd 94.3). Failed heuristics (solve none): 64 of 200 (original), up to 97 in one variant. Removing the example heuristics gave 0 for all.
limits: One model. Large spread (sd about 94) shows results depend heavily on sampling; a single draw is unreliable. Replacing the examples with domain-independent heuristics (goal count, delete-relaxation heuristics) was the weaker variant tested.
agent_relevance: Show worked examples of how to build a simple estimate, sample many, test each, and keep the best. A single try is a lottery.

source: Tuisov, Vernik, Shleyfman (2025) Successor-Generator Planning with LLM-generated Heuristics (arXiv 2501.18784, v5)
finding: Independent extension of the LLM-writes-the-heuristic idea to problems given as code (successor generator, goal test), including numeric and non-PDDL problems. Reaches state-of-the-art coverage; showing the model the concrete instance did not help.
numbers: GPT-4.1, 18 domains x 20 tasks (360): domain-dependent prompt coverage 207 (first compile), 245 (retry until success), 247 (SelfPortfolio-10). With instance-specific prompt: 162, 222, 225. Adding Twin Prime and Pacman (400 tasks): 234, 272, 281 vs 195, 255, 259. Models tested: GPT-4.1, GPT-5.1, Claude Sonnet 4.5 and mini variants. Reimplemented h^md in own planner did worse than ENHSP-20 on some domains.
limits: Instance-specific info lowered coverage with GPT-4.1 (authors guess a stronger model might use it). Weak in domains with opaque names or goals (Pathways, Settlers). Also, LLM heuristics were compared in a different planner implementation, so representation effects are not fully ruled out.
agent_relevance: A second team reproduced the main effect with different models and a code interface. Giving more detail about the specific problem hurt, so the relaxed estimate should be general to the problem type.

source: Katz, Kokel, Srinivas, Sohrabi (2024/2026) Thought of Search: Planning with Language Models Through The Lens of Efficiency
finding: Instead of calling an LLM at every search step, ask it for the code of the successor function and goal test once, then run ordinary sound search. Perfect accuracy on four datasets with a handful of LLM calls. They did not generate a heuristic and left that for later.
numbers: 24 game: 1362 problems, 100% solved; Tree-of-Thoughts reports 75% on a 100-problem subset using many calls. State space for 24 game is at most 4573 states per instance. Mini crosswords, Blocksworld, PrOntoQA also solved fully. Competing LLM-in-the-loop methods explore a very small share of the space (one to two orders of magnitude less than the sound search in 24 game and crosswords).
limits: Small, bounded search spaces. Needs a formal model of the problem; the paper says heuristic generation is future work.
agent_relevance: For problems with a checkable model, move from 'model thinks every step' to 'model writes the checker and the simple solver once'. Matches the evidence in b17.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models (NeurIPS 2023)
finding: Model rates partial solutions as sure, maybe or impossible by short look-ahead, used as a heuristic to prune a search tree. Large gains on Game of 24 and crosswords.
numbers: Game of 24 (GPT-4): IO 7.3%, CoT 4.0%, CoT-SC 9.0%, ToT breadth 1: 45%, breadth 5: 74%. CoT best of 100 samples: 49%. IO + refine (k=10): 27%. About 60% of CoT samples already fail at the first step. Crosswords: word-level success 60% vs under 16% for IO/CoT; 4 of 20 games solved (7/20 with oracle best state). Ablations: no pruning worse; no backtracking 20% word-level.
limits: Follow-up by Katz et al. (b21) shows plain search with code beats it on the same tasks. The evaluator is imperfect: it pruned words in solved crosswords. Costs about 5.5 to 6.7k extra tokens per task vs CoT.
agent_relevance: The model's own quick 'can this still work?' judgment works as a lookahead heuristic, but it is noisy and prunes true solutions. Needs a re-check path for pruned branches.

source: Zheng et al. (2023) Take a Step Back: Evoking Reasoning via Abstraction in Large Language Models (ICLR 2024)
finding: Asking the model first for the general principle or higher-level question, then answering the original, helps most on physics, chemistry and temporal facts. It is abstraction rather than relaxation, and the gain is smaller on strong models and easy tasks.
numbers: PaLM-2L: MMLU Physics 66.4% to 73.2%, Chemistry 70.9% to 81.8%; TimeQA 41.5% to 66.0% (68.7% with RAG); MuSiQue about +7 points. GPT-4: Physics 69.4% to 84.5%, Chemistry 80.9% to 85.6%, but GPT-4 + CoT was 82.9% and 85.3%. StrategyQA baseline already 82.8%, no significant gain from CoT or TDB. Error analysis on Physics: fixes 20.5% of baseline errors, adds 11.9% new ones. Step-Back accuracy rose with one example, not more.
limits: Not planning. Reasoning step stays the main error source. Authors' own paper, same group as the models. Against GPT-4 + CoT the gain on Physics is small (84.5 vs 82.9).
agent_relevance: Closest measured LLM analogue to 'solve the easier, more abstract version first', with a net gain of about 8 to 25 points on some tasks, but a 12% rate of new errors. Use as one operator, not a default.

source: Zhou et al. (2023) Least-to-Most Prompting Enables Complex Reasoning in Large Language Models (ICLR 2023)
finding: Break a hard problem into easier sub-problems solved in order, with each answer fed into the next. Large gain over chain-of-thought on length generalization, where CoT fails.
numbers: SCAN length split, code-davinci-002: standard 16.7%, CoT 16.2%, least-to-most 99.7%. text-davinci-002: 6.0, 0.0, 76.0. code-davinci-001: 0.4, 0.0, 60.7. Uses 14 exemplars. Last-letter concatenation: CoT falls with list length while least-to-most holds.
limits: Decomposition into easier parts, not removal of a constraint. SCAN is a synthetic task. Gains depend on the model (code-davinci-002 best). Stechly et al. (b16) found similar example-specific limits for CoT in planning.
agent_relevance: Decompose and solve in order works when sub-problems share structure with the examples shown. Easier-first ordering is supported; a dropped-constraint version is not tested here.

source: Meng et al. (2024) LLM A*: Human in the Loop Large Language Models Enabled A* Search for Robotics
finding: The LLM is given the grid, costs and the Manhattan distance heuristic and picks next nodes in an A* style loop. Claims paths close to A* with a smaller search space and better than reinforcement learning.
numbers: No exact figures extracted from the text I read; the abstract says paths 'comparable to A*' with reduced search space. Results shown in figures and tables I did not parse number by number.
limits: Small grid path planning, evidence is thin and not extracted in detail. Manhattan distance is a classic relaxation (ignore walls), but the paper does not test that choice. Low confidence. Only the abstract and skim read, so marked not opened.
agent_relevance: Weak evidence. Shows that a ready-made relaxed estimate (Manhattan distance) can be given to a model as context. Needs our own test before relying on it.

source: Cross-source synthesis on failures of relaxed estimates (b02, b04, b08, b14, b18)
finding: Across the sources read, relaxed estimates fail in three repeatable ways: they cannot see dead ends caused by the dropped constraint, extra accuracy has diminishing returns for optimal search, and the benefit depends on how the problem class is shaped.
numbers: FF: unsolved Mystery and Mprime tasks end in dead ends (b02). Hoffmann: 6 of 30 domains have unrecognized dead ends (b04). Almost-perfect heuristic still exponential (b08). R1 heuristic worse than h_FF on Floortile (b18).
limits: This line is my own summary of lines I opened, not a separate source. Marked opened:false for that reason.
agent_relevance: Design rule for O4: before dropping a constraint, name which dead ends it could hide, and keep a check for exactly that.

source: Gap statement: direct tests of LLMs solving a relaxed problem to rank candidate moves
finding: I found no paper that measures an LLM dropping a constraint, solving the easy version and using that result to rank real search children. The measured LLM work either has the LLM write a heuristic function (b17, b20), write search code (b21), score partial states (b22), or abstract the question (b23).
numbers: Searches run on 2026-10-26: WebSearch on relaxed-problem LLM planning heuristics, and arXiv/PlanBench reading. Nothing found; not a proof of absence.
limits: Search was limited in time. Could be missed work in 2025 to 2026 literature.
agent_relevance: Our own test is needed. The SUBFIELDS question (does the relaxed result predict the child's test result) has no outside answer yet.
